title: Photosynthesis: the light lab
subtitle: Predict a pattern, inspect the method and explain the evidence
objective: Describe photosynthesis and investigate how light intensity affects a measured proxy for its rate.

sow.alignment: Directly develops C36 and Pearson 6.2,6.3 and core practical 6.5. Supplied data support planning/analysis if a practical cannot run; they do not count as pupils personally completing a practical. Inverse-square calculations are not required.

priorLearning: A fair comparison changes one intended variable.
Rate means an amount or change per unit time.
success: State the reactants, products and energy source for photosynthesis.
Explain a fair light investigation with a measured outcome and controls.
Calculate a mean bubble rate and explain its limitation as a proxy.

vocabulary.meaning: Using light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen.
A pigment that absorbs light in photosynthesis.
How much happens in a stated time.
A measurement used to indicate another quantity, with limitations.
A factor kept the same to make a comparison fairer.
A factor in short supply that restricts the rate of a process.

equipment: Printed shared evidence and one selected response route; pen, ruler and calculator.
Projector or offline HTML/PowerPoint. Optional word processor or spreadsheet.
Optional supervised demonstration: school-approved aquatic plant, transparent vessel on tray, same dilute sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, cool LED lamp, ruler, timer and thermometer.
Optional light sensor/data logger with lux display; never rely on distance alone as a direct intensity measurement.
preparation: Print the shared evidence page, one chosen response route and exit page. Routes are alternatives, not a workload ladder.
Read the teacher answers before teaching. All numerical sample data in this lesson are constructed for learning.

The paper/data route is complete. If demonstrating, technician/teacher prepares an approved pondweed shoot with a fresh cut under water and checks bubbling before the lesson. Do not acquire or release invasive species.

Keep the same shoot, solution volume/concentration, counting interval and background light. Let the shoot adjust for at least 2 minutes after a light change; monitor temperature. Record actual results separately from constructed values.

For data logging, position the light sensor consistently beside the vessel facing the lamp; log one reading each second for 30 seconds at each position and record the mean. Lux is a practical light indicator, not a direct measurement of photosynthetic photon flux.
safety: Use the fully supplied paper route if apparatus is not prepared. No flames, gas tests or hot-lamp practical is required.
Teacher handles cutting and fragile glass. Keep electrical equipment away from water; use a stable tray and school-approved lamp setup.
Do not taste solution or plant material. Wash hands after handling and dispose of plant material according to school procedures; never release it outdoors.
practicalAlternative: Analyse the supplied constructed table and apparatus diagram. Pupils make the same predictions, controls and evidence-based conclusions without using water, plants or electrical equipment.

misconceptions.claim: Light is a material reactant that becomes oxygen.
misconceptions.correction: Light supplies energy; carbon dioxide and water are reactants, glucose and oxygen are products.
misconceptions.check: Ask pupils to put light over the reaction arrow.

misconceptions.claim: A bubble count is an exact oxygen volume.
misconceptions.correction: Bubble sizes can differ and some gas dissolves; the count is an imperfect proxy.
misconceptions.check: Compare one large bubble with two small ones.

misconceptions.claim: Changing lamp distance changes only light.
misconceptions.correction: It can also change heating; monitor temperature and use a cool source/appropriate control.
misconceptions.check: Ask which measurement checks an unwanted temperature change.

misconceptions.claim: More light always increases photosynthesis without limit.
misconceptions.correction: At higher light another factor can limit the rate; the supplied range is not a universal rule.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether three conditions justify an unlimited prediction.

access.supported: Same core scientific goal, with word bank, short prompts, read-aloud or pointing/dictation. Do not assign a route from diagnosis.
access.standard: Use the supplied evidence to explain and justify an independent scientific decision.
access.stretch: Optional challenge after secure core: evaluate a limitation and transfer the science. Higher-tier-only material, where present, is labelled explicitly.
access.regulation: Preview the sequence. Offer solo or partner work, a pass and quiet response. Allow a brief reset and re-entry at the next numbered task; no compulsory disclosure, performance or speed competition.

slides.title: Can light change what a plant makes?
body: Mission: make a prediction, test the method and defend a conclusion.
A good investigation records a limit as well as a pattern.
slides.notes: Ask pupils to predict the effect of moving the lamp closer. State that this is a planned or supervised comparison, not a race to produce the most bubbles.

slides.title: Materials, energy and measurement
body: R1. Where is chlorophyll found in plant cells?
R2. What does a control variable do?
R3. What does “per minute” tell us?
slides.notes: R1 chloroplasts. R2 kept the same to improve fairness. R3 a 60-second interval. If pupils say plant food comes from soil, revisit glucose production in the next diagram.

slides.title: Read the reaction accurately
body: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen.
Light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll.
Photosynthesis takes in energy.
slides.notes: Think aloud: “I list matter on the two sides and put energy above the arrow. Glucose is a product, not a soil nutrient. Plants also respire; this reaction is not their only process.” Teach endothermic as takes in energy without requiring a balanced symbol equation.

visual.title: Matter changes; light supplies the energy
visual.description: Photosynthesis word equation. Carbon dioxide and water are converted into glucose and oxygen using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll. The process takes in energy; light is not a material reactant.

elements.text: Matter changes; light supplies the energy

Glucose can build biomass or be used in respiration.
Photosynthesis takes in energy.

slides.title: I plan the measurement before moving the lamp
body: Change the light level and record it.
Count bubbles over equal one-minute intervals.
Keep the shoot and other conditions comparable.
slides.notes: Model check: same shoot and solution; at least 2 minutes adjustment; one-minute counts repeated three times; temperature monitored and kept comparable. Use sensor consistently. A cooler lamp reduces a heating confound, but does not remove the need to check.

visual.title: Change light; monitor temperature
visual.description: Schematic supervised pondweed setup with LED lamp, distance ruler, vessel of solution, shoot, bubbles, light sensor and thermometer. It models apparatus positions, not a scale drawing or an exact gas-volume method.

elements.text: Same shoot, solution, timing and background light.

slides.title: Work a rate and a mean
body: Worked example:12 bubbles in 2 minutes =6 per minute.
Three one-minute counts 4,5,6 have mean 5.
Count is a proxy, not an exact oxygen volume.
slides.notes: Model 12÷2=6 bubbles/min. Then(4+5+6)÷3=5. These are constructed examples. Explain differing bubble sizes and dissolved gas. A gas-volume measurement over time can improve the proxy, but it still needs controlled conditions.

visual.title: Constructed results: compare mean bubble rates
visual.description: Constructed sample means: at 300 lux 5 bubbles/min,600 lux 10 bubbles/min,1200 lux 17 bubbles/min. The categorical axis represents measured light levels. Bubble count is a proxy, not exact oxygen volume.

slides.title: Investigation team: predict, then calculate
body: W1. Predict the largest mean rate.
Calculate the mean for each light level.
slides.notes: Use supplied data or own demonstration data with labels kept distinct. Constructed means 5,10,17. Ask pupils whether the measured lux values support the closer-lamp prediction; do not introduce a proportional-distance rule.

table.caption: Constructed sample data; same shoot/solution and 20°C; counts are bubbles.

slides.title: Method repair challenge
body: W2. A group changes the shoot and the lamp position together.
Can it isolate the light effect? Repair one step.
slides.notes: No: differences in shoot length/leaf area/activity may change bubbling. Keep same shoot or matched replicates and change intended light level only, while monitoring temperature and other controls. Ask a pupil to justify what the repair isolates.

visual.description: Schematic supervised pondweed setup with LED lamp, distance ruler, vessel of solution, shoot, bubbles, light sensor and thermometer. It models apparatus positions, not a scale drawing or an exact gas-volume method.

elements.text: Same shoot, solution, timing and background light.

slides.title: Which conclusion earns its claim?
body: W3. “Within this range, higher measured light gave a higher mean count.”
Does that prove unlimited growth or exact oxygen volume?
slides.notes: It supports the observed count pattern in these conditions. It does not establish unlimited response, exact oxygen volume or plant growth. Ask for the missing measurement needed to claim growth.
slides.reveal: Mean count rises 5→10→17 bubbles/min in this constructed range. Other limiting factors and proxy limits remain.

slides.title: A valid scientific conclusion
body: Choose the statement supported by the method.
slides.notes: B correct. Return to reaction if A, bubble limitation if C, controls if D.

options.text: Oxygen is made from light as a material.
options.feedback: Light supplies energy; carbon dioxide and water are the material reactants.

options.text: Bubble count can indicate a pattern, but bubble size limits precision.
options.feedback: Yes. Count is a proxy; equal counts need not mean equal oxygen volume.

options.text: Twice the bubbles always means exactly twice the oxygen volume.
options.feedback: Bubble sizes can differ and some oxygen dissolves.

options.text: Changing the shoot and light together isolates light.
options.feedback: The shoot change is another possible cause of a count difference.

slides.title: Prepare your investigation brief
body: Choose your response route.
Include a reaction, method and evidence-based conclusion.
slides.notes: Provide shared data, selected route and calculator. A labelled diagram or oral explanation can show the same core understanding.

slides.title: Use the evidence independently
body: Predict → calculate → explain → improve the method.
Keep constructed results separate from any actual observations.
slides.notes: Supported S1–S4; standard M1–M4; stretch T1–T4. Check rate units and control reasoning. Do not award an unsupported claim that light always remains limiting.

slides.title: Audience question: what did you measure?
body: L1. Show your conclusion.
Audience asks: “Count, volume, growth or photosynthesis itself?”
slides.notes: Pupil names the measured bubble count and explains its use as proxy; revise overclaim. Teacher/TA can be a quiet audience.

slides.title: A strong brief names its limitation
body: The reaction explains the process.
The method determines what the evidence can show.
slides.notes: Model: “More measured light was associated with higher mean bubble counts under matched conditions. Bubble size and dissolved gas limit how exactly counts show oxygen production.”

slides.title: Keep matter, energy and evidence distinct
body: E1. Name the two material reactants.
E2. Calculate 15 bubbles in 3 minutes.
E3. Name one control and one proxy limit.
slides.notes: E1 carbon dioxide/water. E2=5 bubbles/min. E3 same shoot/solution/temp/timing; bubble size or gas dissolving. Use errors to identify next practical support.

slides.title: Next useful step
body: Reaction • rate • fair method • cautious conclusion.
slides.notes: Shared exit minute; accept labelled arrows instead of prose.

pupilPages.title: Shared evidence | Light investigation
pupilPages.intro: Constructed sample data. Same shoot, solution, one-minute intervals and 20°C water. Sensor readings are mean lux at the vessel; lux is a practical light indicator.

blocks.text: Method: use prepared shoot and same solution. Set light position; allow at least 2 minutes to adjust. Monitor temperature. Take three equal one-minute counts. For logging: sensor faces lamp in the same orientation; record once each second for 30 seconds and take its mean. Repeat at each position.
Paper route: analyse these values only. Optional demonstration uses teacher-prepared apparatus; record any real observations separately. Bubble sizes vary and some oxygen remains dissolved.

blocks.prompt: W1. Predict and calculate means. W2. Repair the two-variable method. W3. State a supported conclusion.

pupilPages.title: Supported route | Build the brief
pupilPages.intro: Word bank: carbon dioxide; water; glucose; oxygen; light; same; rate; proxy.

blocks.prompt: S1. Write the photosynthesis word equation. Put the energy source above the arrow.
S2. Calculate each mean bubble count. Show one addition and division.
S3. Name what changes and two things kept the same. Why keep them the same?
S4. Describe the pattern with two values. State one reason counts are not exact oxygen volumes.

pupilPages.title: Standard route | Investigation proposal
pupilPages.intro: Use the constructed table and precise units.

blocks.prompt: M1. State the photosynthesis word equation and explain the role of light/chlorophyll.
M2. Calculate all means and compare the lowest/highest light levels numerically.
M3. Describe a reproducible method: intended variable, measured outcome, timing/repeats, controls and sensor use.
M4. Write a supported conclusion and one improvement to the oxygen measurement. Explain why it helps.

pupilPages.title: Stretch route | How strong is the evidence?
pupilPages.intro: Optional extension. A second constructed trial at 1200 lux gives one-minute counts 16,17,35. A note says the third bubble count may include two minutes of observation.

blocks.prompt: T1. Calculate the mean of all three counts. Explain why the timing note matters before accepting it.
T2. Describe a fair way to investigate the suspicious result without deleting it just because it is different.
T3. A light sensor rises further but the mean count stops rising. Suggest a possible limiting factor and a test that changes only that factor.
T4. Explain why lux and bubble counts are useful indicators but neither is a direct measurement of glucose production.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection | Process and measurement
pupilPages.intro: Use one accurate sentence for each distinction.

blocks.prompt: E1. Name the two material reactants in photosynthesis.
E2. 15 bubbles in 3 minutes: show the rate calculation and unit.
E3. Give one control variable and one limitation of the bubble proxy.
L1. What did your audience ask? Improve one claim or measurement label.

answers.label: Retrieval
answers.answer: R1 chloroplasts. R2 a factor kept the same to improve fairness. R3 each 60 seconds.

answers.label: W1–W3
answers.answer: W1 means 5,10,17 bubbles/min at 300,600,1200 lux. W2 use the same shoot/matched replicates and change the intended light level only, controlling temperature and solution. W3 count rises with measured light in this range; no unlimited-growth or exact-volume claim is justified.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: A false: light is energy, not a material reactant. B true: count indicates a pattern with bubble-size limitations. C false: different bubble sizes/dissolved gas. D false: changing shoots introduces another variable.

answers.label: S1 / M1
answers.answer: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, with light energy absorbed by chlorophyll. Photosynthesis takes in energy; glucose can contribute to biomass or respiration.

answers.label: S2 / M2
answers.answer: (4+5+6)/3=5;(9+10+11)/3=10;(16+17+18)/3=17 bubbles/min. From 300 to 1200 lux the mean increases by 12 bubbles/min. This is the observed range, not a universal proportionality.

answers.label: S3 / M3
answers.answer: Change measured light level using lamp position. Count bubbles for equal one-minute intervals; repeat three times after adjustment. Same shoot, solution volume/concentration, background light and comparable temperature. Sensor orientation/location consistent; optional 30 second logging mean. Controls reduce alternative explanations.

answers.label: S4 / M4
answers.answer: Higher measured light is associated with higher mean count here, for example 300 lux→5 and 1200 lux→17 bubbles/min. Counts do not equal exact gas volumes because sizes differ and gas may dissolve. Collect gas volume over a fixed time with appropriate apparatus to reduce the bubble-size limitation; maintain other controls.

answers.label: T1
answers.answer: (16+17+35)/3=68/3≈22.7 bubbles/min only if all counts were truly one minute. If the 35 count lasted two minutes, averaging raw counts as equal rates is invalid. The note is uncertain; check the record before recalculating.

answers.label: T2
answers.answer: Retain and annotate the original record; verify timing or repeat matched measurements with a clear timer/observer. Do not silently delete an inconvenient value or assume the cause from its size alone.

answers.label: T3
answers.answer: Carbon dioxide availability or temperature could limit the rate. Example: compare matched carbon dioxide availability at the same light and temperature with repeats. The plateau alone does not identify which factor is limiting.

answers.label: T4
answers.answer: Lux measures light weighted to human visual sensitivity, not glucose production or exact photosynthetic photon flux. Bubble counts indicate gas release, with volume/dissolution limits; glucose itself is not measured.

answers.label: Exit and assessment
answers.answer: E1 carbon dioxide and water. E2 15÷3=5 bubbles/min. E3 valid controlled factor plus bubble-size/dissolved-gas limit. L1 accepts a specific evidence-based revision or justified label. Secure core = correct reaction, fair variable logic and proxy-aware conclusion.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2, retrieval 3, I do 10, We do 7, hinge 3, independent 11, review 3, exit 1. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Choose one response route. Accept accurate speech, pointing plus explanation, annotations or writing as evidence.
A quiet review still has an audience: teacher or TA reads the pupil’s decision, asks one evidence question, and the pupil revises or confirms it.

Optional apparatus is a supervised demonstration/practical route only after local preparation. The complete supplied data route teaches planning and analysis; do not record it as pupils having personally completed a core practical.

Interactive We do uses the exact three constructed light/count conditions. Predict which condition gives the greatest mean, test the result, then check whether the method isolates light. Paper W1–W3 uses the same table. Any animated bubbles illustrate a constructed count, not a physiological simulation.
